clinicalPearls: The commonest type of urinary stone; typically presents with acute loin-to-groin colic accompanied by haematuria, nausea and a restless patient unable to find a comfortable position
The principal metabolic drivers are hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, hypocitraturia and a persistently low urine volume
Stones are radio-opaque and usually visible on plain imaging, but non-contrast CT is the diagnostic standard for confirming and localising them
Urine microscopy classically shows bipyramidal (envelope-shaped) calcium oxalate dihydrate crystals
A full metabolic evaluation with repeated 24-hour urine collections is indicated in recurrent stone-formers to target preventive therapy
General prevention rests on a generous fluid intake to keep the urine dilute, moderating dietary sodium and animal protein, and maintaining a normal dietary calcium intake
Thiazide diuretics lower urinary calcium and potassium citrate corrects hypocitraturia, both reducing recurrence in selected patients
Restricting dietary calcium is counterproductive because it frees intestinal oxalate for absorption and raises urinary oxalate
reference.pathophysiology: Calcium oxalate stones form when the urine becomes supersaturated with calcium and oxalate, permitting crystal nucleation, growth and aggregation. Many stones begin on Randall's plaques, deposits of calcium phosphate in the papillary interstitium that erode through the urothelium and provide a scaffold for calcium oxalate to accrete. Crystallisation is promoted by high urinary calcium and oxalate and by concentrated urine, while citrate and magnesium act as natural inhibitors that complex calcium and oxalate; deficiency of these inhibitors, particularly hypocitraturia, tips the balance toward stone formation. High animal-protein and sodium intake, metabolic acidosis and low fluid intake together create a lithogenic urinary environment.
additionalDifferentials: Uric acid stones, which are radiolucent
Renal or ureteric urothelial tumour causing haematuria
Musculoskeletal or biliary pain mimicking renal colic
additionalInvestigations: Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder to confirm and localise the stone
Analysis of any retrieved stone by infrared spectroscopy or X-ray diffraction
Two 24-hour urine collections measuring volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium and pH
Serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone to exclude primary hyperparathyroidism
Urine microscopy for crystalluria and dipstick for haematuria
Serum urea, electrolytes and creatinine to assess renal function
redFlags: Fever or systemic sepsis with an obstructing stone, indicating an infected obstructed kidney that is a urological emergency
Acute kidney injury, or obstruction of a solitary or transplanted kidney
Intractable pain or persistent vomiting requiring admission
reference.prognosis: With adequate fluid intake and targeted metabolic treatment the recurrence rate falls substantially, but untreated stone-formers have a high likelihood of a further stone within a few years, and repeated obstruction or intervention can contribute to chronic kidney disease.
pitfalls: Advising a low-calcium diet, which increases oxalate absorption and worsens stone formation
Omitting a metabolic evaluation in patients with recurrent stones
Overlooking primary hyperparathyroidism as a treatable cause of hypercalciuria
Attributing all loin pain to a stone and missing an infected obstructed system
management: Relieve acute renal colic with NSAID analgesia, adding an antiemetic and an opioid where pain is severe
Offer medical expulsive therapy with an alpha-blocker to aid spontaneous passage of a distal ureteric stone
Refer for urological stone removal by ureteroscopy, extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy when the stone is large, obstructing or fails to pass
Prevent recurrence with a generous daily fluid intake to keep urine dilute, alongside moderation of dietary sodium and animal protein while maintaining normal dietary calcium
Target the metabolic abnormality found on 24-hour urine testing: a thiazide diuretic for hypercalciuria, potassium citrate for hypocitraturia and reduced oxalate intake for hyperoxaluria
Monitor with repeat 24-hour urine studies, renal function and imaging to detect recurrent or residual stones
Escalate urgently for decompression with a ureteric stent or nephrostomy when obstruction is complicated by infection or deteriorating renal function
